rows.title: Judge Hands Down Harshest Penalty Yet From College Admissions Scandal
rows.standfirst: Prosecutors told the court that they considered Douglas Hodge, the ex-CEO of PIMCO, among the "most culpable" of the parents charged. He has been sentenced to nine months in prison.

rows.title: Jobs Friday: The Racial Unemployment Gap
rows.standfirst: The unemployment rate for black workers is roughly twice that of white workers - and has been for half a century. Today we discuss the reasons for the gap, and how to shrink it.

rows.title: From Delivery Trucks To Scooter-Moving Vans, Fleets Are Going Electric
rows.standfirst: Lime is all about electric vehicles — battery-powered scooters, that is. But now the company is also going to use plug-in vans for behind-the-scenes operations. And it's far from alone.

rows.title: Hiring Picks Up As Employers Add 225,000 Jobs In January
rows.standfirst: U.S. employers added more jobs than expected last month, while the unemployment rate inched up to 3.6%. Unusually warm weather contributed to job gains for construction workers.

rows.title: Betting On The Oscars
rows.standfirst: Betting on the Oscars is now legal in New Jersey and Indiana, so we went down to Atlantic City to place a bet on Best Picture. And we spoke to a few experts beforehand to understand how to make a better bet.

rows.title: Bernie Madoff Seeks Early Release Because He Has 'Less Than 18 Months' To Live
rows.standfirst: A lawyer says Madoff, who is serving a 150-year sentence, suffers from terminal kidney failure. The Federal Bureau of Prisons denied a similar request for release last year.

rows.title: Cities And States Are Saying No To Cashless Shops
rows.standfirst: Washington, D.C., is the latest city to consider banning businesses from rejecting cash. Opponents of cashless stores say they discriminate against low-income, homeless and undocumented people.

rows.title: China Will Cut Tariffs In Half On $75 Billion Of U.S. Products
rows.standfirst: The reduced tariffs are to take effect next Feb. 14. The move comes after the Trump administration agreed to halve tariffs on about $112 billion in Chinese goods.

rows.title: Triple-A Ratings Are So Yesterday
rows.standfirst: It used to be that companies strove for the best credit rating possible. Today, however, almost everyone's happy to slide by with a barely passing grade.

rows.title: Small Change
rows.standfirst: How fast is the world really changing? The answer affects everything from how we live, to whether robots really will take all our jobs. | Subscribe to our weekly newsletter here.

rows.title: Canadian Court Clears The Way For Trans Mountain Pipeline Expansion
rows.standfirst: The court said the government has adequately consulted with indigenous groups about the pipeline expansion. First Nations have said that they remain concerned about the project's environmental impact.

rows.title: Coronavirus Puts A Crimp On The Chinese Tourism Industry
rows.standfirst: Fear of the respiratory virus, which has infected more than 28,000 people in over two dozen countries, has brought the normally lucrative business to a screeching halt.

rows.title: Macy's Closing 125 Stores, Cutting 2,000 Jobs As Mall Stores Struggle
rows.standfirst: The cuts and closures are part of the Macy's attempt to stabilize its finances and rethink its future. It's also trying out smaller stores outside of malls.

rows.title: Graduates Of Historically Black Colleges May Be Paying More For Loans: Watchdog Group
rows.standfirst: Graduates of historically black or predominantly Hispanic colleges might be paying more to borrow money because of where they went to school, according to a report from a financial watchdog.

rows.title: Kobe Bryant Merchandise Increases In Value But Not Everyone Is Cashing In
rows.standfirst: Shops that sell Kobe Bryant merchandise have seen a spike in sales in the wake of his death. Now they're making a choice: profit from tragedy or keep Bryant's merchandise accessible to the public.

rows.title: The CryptoQueen
rows.standfirst: A mysterious woman promises a financial revolution. That promise leads to greed, corruption and... a beauty pageant. | Subscribe to our weekly newsletter here.

rows.title: How Economists Do Valentines
rows.standfirst: It's an Economic Valentine! Economics isn't known as a language of love. But economists Betsey Stevenson and Justin Wolfers say it's central to their relationship and to their decisions as a couple.

rows.title: U.S. Prosecutors Hit Huawei With New Federal Charges
rows.standfirst: The Department of Justice is accusing the Chinese telecom giant of racketeering and conspiracy to steal trade secrets from U.S. companies. The Trump administration has security concerns about Huawei.

rows.title: For Rent: Fast Fashion
rows.standfirst: Buy or rent? That's becoming a question for manufacturers of more and more types of products. Now fast fashion brands are trying to get in on the movement, too.

rows.title: Filmmaker Tracks Bezos' 'Rise And Reign' And How Amazon Became 'Inescapable'
rows.standfirst: Director James Jacoby catalogs the reach of the tech giant in his new PBS Frontline documentary, Amazon Empire. "So much power is pooled into the hands of one company and one man," he says.

rows.title: Can I date that co-worker? What to consider before an office romance
rows.standfirst: The workplace still ranks as one of the top five places where people meet their mates. Love is intoxicating, but you don't want a workplace romance to become toxic.

rows.title: 'Miami Herald,' 'Kansas City Star' Publisher McClatchy Files For Bankruptcy
rows.standfirst: The company, which operates 30 newsrooms in 14 states, announced a Chapter 11 restructuring. Saddled with debt and pension obligations, McClatchy said it will operate as normal during the process.

rows.title: Our Valentines 2020
rows.standfirst: We're sending valentines to books, ideas, and other stuff we love. | Subscribe to our weekly newsletter here.

rows.title: The First Milestone In The History of Economics
rows.standfirst: The first milestone in the history of economics was an 8th century B.C. poem — a lecture by an ancient Greek poet to his deadbeat brother.

rows.title: Major Smartphone Trade Show Canceled In Barcelona Amid Coronavirus Concerns
rows.standfirst: Organizers have called off the annual Mobile World Congress in Spain after a slew of high-profile tech companies pulled out, citing concerns over the spreading coronavirus outbreak.

rows.title: After Iowa Debacle, Tech Experts Who Aid Progressives Call For A Strategic Shake-Up
rows.standfirst: The failure of this year's Iowa caucuses was years in the making, some technology specialists argue, in part because of the haphazard way political users buy software.

rows.title: The Hope And Hype Of Diabetic Alert Dogs
rows.standfirst: Companies that sell dogs trained to sniff out life-threatening changes in blood sugar for people with diabetes have faced lawsuits or complaints from some of their customers.

rows.title: Coronavirus Casts A Pall Over Cruise Industry At Height Of Booking Season
rows.standfirst: Tales of life on a ship quarantined in Japan amid a coronavirus outbreak are hurting bookings for the growing cruise line industry. But the industry has shaken off worse crises, an analyst says.

rows.title: Why Cheap Solar Could Save the World
rows.standfirst: In the last fifteen years, the cost of solar energy has declined so sharply that it has recently become the cheapest form of energy in the world. Now, major companies are jumping in to invest, but will the markets follow?

rows.title: Whither The Deficit Hawk: Changing Attitudes On Budget Red Ink Among The GOP
rows.standfirst: William Hoagland, who for years helped shape GOP budget policy, says the public just doesn't see rising deficits as a major issue at a time when the economy is doing well.

rows.title: Michael Milken
rows.standfirst: Michael Milken once made $550 million in one year. Then, he went to prison. This week, the President pardoned him. | Subscribe to our weekly newsletter here.

rows.title: The Indicator The Candidates Should Be Talking About
rows.standfirst: Political Economist Jared Bernstein watched this week's Democratic debate. Many economic issues came up, but he thinks the candidates need to start talking about how much U.S. households are saving.

rows.title: Wells Fargo Paying $3 Billion To Settle U.S. Case Over Fraudulent Customer Accounts
rows.standfirst: The bank agreed to settle charges brought by the Justice Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission over accounts, debit cards and other products that customers did not request.

rows.title: Enjoy The Extra Day Off! More Bosses Give 4-Day Workweek A Try
rows.standfirst: The notion of a shorter workweek might sound crazy to overworked Americans, but around the world, companies and even governments are starting to embrace it. The key is fewer meetings and distractions.

rows.title: Forever 21 Filed For Bankruptcy But Will Live On With New Owners
rows.standfirst: Three companies have announced that they are acquiring the retailer aimed at teens and young people, and plan to continue to operate its U.S. and international stores.

rows.title: Timecard Capitalists
rows.standfirst: People who make the highest salaries are increasingly the same people who draw the highest incomes from their capital.

rows.title: The Most Dangerous Economist
rows.standfirst: When the US needed a spy plane and an invasion, it hired the economist Richard Bissell.

rows.title: Disparities In Government Contracting Hurt Minority-Owned Businesses
rows.standfirst: Despite affirmative action goals meant to make up for disparities, white-owned businesses win most of the bids for government work. And in many places the numbers are getting worse.

rows.title: Meet Our Junk Bond!
rows.standfirst: Last year, Team Indicator bought a junk bond! The bond was from a company called Hornbeck Offshore Services. On today's show, we learn more about the company and we check in on our investment.

rows.title: Indicate This
rows.standfirst: From our daily podcast The Indicator: How Amazon Prime packages reach you so damn fast? And why Lancaster, PA became the refugee capital of America?

rows.title: Hunt For New Coronavirus Treatments Includes Gene-Silencing And Monoclonal Antibodies
rows.standfirst: The new coronavirus has spurred biotech labs in universities and companies to try to find new approaches to stopping the virus — from blocking its key enzymes to interfering with its genetics.

rows.title: The Wide-Ranging Ways In Which The Coronavirus Is Hurting Global Business
rows.standfirst: Some factories are beginning to reopen, but labor shortages continue. In a recent poll of U.S. companies by Shanghai's American Chamber of Commerce, 78% said they lack staff to resume full production.

rows.title: China Expels 3 'Wall Street Journal' Reporters, Citing 'Racist' Headline
rows.standfirst: The move comes a day after the U.S. State Department designated five Chinese state media outlets as foreign government missions, thus treating them as extensions of Beijing.

rows.title: It's Not Just Hospitals That Are Quick To Sue Patients Who Can't Pay
rows.standfirst: The firm that staffed the emergency room with doctors at Nashville General Hospital was taking more patients to court for unpaid medical bills than any other hospital or practice in the city.

rows.title: Listener Questions: Minimum Wage & Gender-Fluid Tadpoles
rows.standfirst: Cardiff takes on the national debt, minimum wage, and gender-fluid tadpoles to get answers to your burning questions.

rows.title: Joe Coulombe, Founder And Namesake Of Trader Joe's, Dies At 89
rows.standfirst: The original Trader Joe, who died Friday, opened the first store in 1967 with oddball nautical decor and a guiding principle: "Trader Joe's is for overeducated and underpaid people."

rows.title: As New Coronavirus Cases Slow In China, Factories Start Reopening
rows.standfirst: Strict quarantine measures have prevented 300 million migrant workers from returning to work. Now local authorities are trying to get businesses going again. The main bottleneck: a shrunken workforce.

rows.title: Coronavirus: A View From Hong Kong
rows.standfirst: As coronavirus fears roiled markets this week, we hear from Bloomberg's Tracy Alloway, who's based in Hong Kong, about what it's like to live in a city in the throes of an outbreak

rows.title: Google Employee Tests Positive For Coronavirus; Company Expands Travel Restrictions
rows.standfirst: American companies are curbing travel and pulling out of big events as they try to limit their employees' exposure to the growing outbreak

rows.title: Wall Street's Brutal Week Slashed Nearly 3,600 Points From Dow
rows.standfirst: The U.S. stock market ended its worst week since the financial crisis with the Dow Jones Industrial Average falling 12.4%. Fed Chairman Jerome Powell promises to support the economy as necessary.

rows.title: Citing Climate Commitments, U.K. Court Blocks New Runway At Heathrow Airport
rows.standfirst: The Court of Appeal said the major international hub's plans for an additional runway failed to consider the government's pledges on carbon emissions. It's a big win for climate activists.

rows.title: How Wealth Has Changed
rows.standfirst: The world has changed, and nearly two thirds of global wealth is human capital. Policymakers and politicians may not understand just what that means for global politics.

rows.title: Dow Falls Nearly 1,200 Points; Stocks Now In Correction Territory
rows.standfirst: Stocks continued their downward slide on Thursday, with major indexes falling 10% below their recent peaks. Investors worry about the economic toll of a widening coronavirus epidemic.

rows.title: Better Late Than Never? Big Companies Scramble To Make Lofty Climate Promises
rows.standfirst: Pressure is mounting on CEOs as everyone from investors to employees sounds the alarm about the climate crisis. Some companies are responding, but even ambitious targets won't be enough on their own.

rows.title: The Rise And Fall (And Rise?) Of NASCAR
rows.standfirst: Last week's Daytona 500 came at a precarious time for NASCAR. Once a behemoth in the world of professional sports, the company is now trying to entice a new generation of race fans.

rows.title: As U.S. Preps For Coronavirus, Health Workers Question Safety Measures
rows.standfirst: The plight of Chinese health care workers contracting the coronavirus has prompted front-line medical staff in the U.S. to wonder if they're protected. Hospitals say they're taking steps to prepare.

rows.title: 'Gives Me Hope': How Low-Paid Workers Rose Up Against Stagnant Wages
rows.standfirst: When some fast-food workers in New York went on strike one morning in 2012, they had no idea it was the beginning of an unusual movement that would propel an economic revolution.

rows.title: Vodka Proof
rows.standfirst: Vodka is the best-selling spirit in the United States, and there are zillions of brands. But is there any difference between them? | Subscribe to our weekly newsletter here.

rows.title: Alaska Feels The Brunt As Investors Promise Retreat On Fossil Fuels
rows.standfirst: JPMorgan Chase is the latest investor to say it won't finance drilling in Alaska's Arctic. Some welcome the move, but there's also concern in a state that depends heavily on oil revenue.

rows.title: Who Needs A Realtor? iBuyers Pay Instant Cash For Your House
rows.standfirst: Companies such as Opendoor, RedfinNow and Zillow will pay cash for your house and buy it quickly. New numbers show these types of sales are growing very quickly, but is it a good idea?
